\iffalse
\begin{itemize}
\item Settling prediction limits throughput in coupled high-precision gantries, so model error has a direct operational cost \cite{garcia2013model}
\item The concrete digital-twin use case is to evaluate relevant ASMPT motion and a changed controller before deployment on the machine
\item The physics model exposes masses, stiffnesses, damping, and coupling, but omits position-dependent flexible dynamics that matter for prediction
\item A black-box model offers flexibility but weakens extrapolation arguments and removes parameters useful for control design, digital twins, and health monitoring
\item Grey-box dynamic augmentation is the target compromise: preserve the baseline and learn only the missing state dynamics \cite{hoekstra2026lfr}
\end{itemize}
\fi

White-box models are attractive because they reflect the physics of the
system, which makes them interpretable.
First-principles (FP) models are a specific type of white-box model,
derived from physical laws and described by quantities such as mass,
stiffness, and damping.
However, purely physics-based models do not always capture all behaviour
needed for accurate prediction across the operating range
\cite{willard2020integrating}.
More accurate FP models can be developed, but this is labour-intensive
\cite{hoekstra2026lfr}.

Grey-box modelling is the logical choice, because it is able to
combine a baseline model with interpretable parameters
\chg[Dirk]{with data-driven flexibility needed}{and a data-driven model}
for accurate prediction
\cite{noel2018greybox}.
Grey-box approaches include parameter
re-estimation within the physics model structure, static residual
correction on the model output, and dynamic augmentation that extends the
baseline with learned states \cite{willard2020integrating, hoekstra2026lfr}.
% NEW: research plan Literature.tex l.1 word for word, citation changed;
%   Willard Secs. 2.3, 3.4.1 (calibration, residual modelling), Hoekstra
%   2026 Sec. 2 (static vs dynamic)
Model augmentation combines a physics-based baseline model with a learned
component, so that the learned component only needs to capture the dynamics
the physics-based model cannot describe \cite{hoekstra2026lfr}\add[own]{,
\cite{retzler2024}}.
% NEW: wording from research plan Literature.tex l.3; Hoekstra 2026 Sec. 1,
%   p. 2

%   "flexible dynamics" dropped: P1 says the system exhibits flexible
%   dynamics and the baseline models the flexible joints (Fig. 1).
Dynamic augmentation is chosen\chg[own]{ to be able to model missing
dynamics, such as flexible dynamics. These}{, because missing dynamics}
require additional states, which
parameter re-estimation
and static output correction cannot provide \cite{hoekstra2026lfr}.

The actuator forces are defined as
$\uact=[F_{X1}\;F_{X2}\;F_Y]^\top$ and the measured positions
$\qact=[X_1\;X_2\;Y]^\top$.
Here $F_{X1}$, $F_{X2}$ and $F_Y$ are the forces and
$X_1$, $X_2$ and $Y$ the measured positions of the
\chg[Dirk]{two X actuators and the Y actuator}{two X and the Y actuators}%
\add[Q17]{\kwtwo{, each from a linear encoder~\cite{garcia2013model}}}.
% FEEDBACK v1 (2026-10-21): Q17 ("add location of encoders"): Garcia Sec.

%   position. Js22 ("positions of what? the stages?"): no change, "of the

\\
The system to be identified is the gantry system
described \chg{as,}{by}
\begin{equation}
  \dot x(t)=f\bigl(x(t),\uact(t)\bigr),\qquad y_k=\qact(kT_s)+v_k,
  \label{eq:system}
\end{equation}
% where the \kw{state $x$ is unknown, except that it contains the actuator
% positions $\qact$}, $y_k$ are the measured positions at sample $k$ with
% sampling time $T_s$, and $v_k$ is zero-mean, coloured measurement noise.
% The state-transition function $f$ is unknown.
where the \chg[own]{\kw{state $x$ is unknown, except that it contains the actuator
positions $\qact$}}{state $x$ contains the actuator positions $\qact$}, $y_k$ are the measured positions at sample $k$ with
sampling time $T_s$, and $v_k$ is zero-mean, coloured measurement noise.
The \chg[own]{state-transition function $f$ is}{function $f$ and the
dimension of $x$ are} unknown.
The system runs in closed loop with an assumed known
linear time-invariant feedback controller\del[M-p3]{ (Section~\ref{sec:aug_loop})},
which gives the data set $\mathcal D_N=\{u_{\mathrm{act},k},y_k\}_{k=1}^N$.
% \add[M-p3]{The controller computes the actuator forces from the reference
% $r_k$ and the measured positions, and a feedforward $u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k$ is
% added (Fig.~\ref{fig:system_loop}):}
\add[M-p3]{The controller computes the actuator forces from the
error between the reference $r_k$ and the measured positions $y_k$,
and a feedforward $u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k$ is added (Fig.~\ref{fig:system_loop}):}
\begin{equation}

\subsection{Closed-loop simulation}\label{sec:aug_loop}
\ifdraft
\begin{itemize}
\item The model is not driven by the recorded input (2026 Eq.~(22)), for two reasons: noise-induced bias under feedback (Kessels Remark~5.6, SUBNET; indirect approach, Forssell and Ljung) and the free axes of Section~\ref{sec:aug_structure}, which violate the stability condition behind SUBNET consistency (Beintema Cond.~1); motivation, not a proof
\item As in Kessels (Eqs.~(5.12), (5.13)), each window is simulated in closed loop with the known controller, which forms its error against the model output; system and model loops share $r$ and $u^{\mathrm{ff}}$
\item The controller is linear and time invariant, so subtracting the system's loop cancels $r$ and $u^{\mathrm{ff}}$; the residual form needs only the recorded $u_{\mathrm{act}}$ and $y$, and is exact when $u_{\mathrm{act}}$ was produced by this controller from $y$ (this work)
\item $x^{c}_\tau=0$ starts the model's controller in the system's controller state, as the encoder does for the plant state; no controller state is estimated, unlike Kessels Remark~5.4 (this work)
\item No plant feedthrough fixes the step order, so $D_{\mathrm{fb}}$ closes no algebraic loop (as Kessels Remark~5.1); one normalised step displayed
\item The output error re-enters the model input, so part of it is corrected within the window; error before $\tau$ is not carried in, the free-run validation carries it
\end{itemize}
\fi

\begin{itemize}
\item The model is not driven by the recorded input (2026 Eq.~(22)), for two reasons: noise-induced bias under feedback (Kessels Remark~5.6, SUBNET; indirect approach, Forssell and Ljung) and the free axes of Section~\ref{sec:aug_structure}, which violate the stability condition behind SUBNET consistency (Beintema Cond.~1); motivation, not a proof
\item As in Kessels (Eqs.~(5.12), (5.13)), each window is simulated in closed loop with the known controller, which forms its error against the model output; system and model loops share $r$ and $u^{\mathrm{ff}}$
\item The controller is linear and time invariant, so subtracting the system's loop cancels $r$ and $u^{\mathrm{ff}}$; the residual form needs only the recorded $u_{\mathrm{act}}$ and $y$, and is exact when $u_{\mathrm{act}}$ was produced by this controller from $y$ (this work)
\item $x^{c}_\tau=0$ starts the model's controller in the system's controller state, as the encoder does for the plant state; no controller state is estimated, unlike Kessels Remark~5.4 (this work)
\item No plant feedthrough fixes the step order, so $D_{\mathrm{fb}}$ closes no algebraic loop (as Kessels Remark~5.1); one normalised step displayed
\item The output error re-enters the model input, so part of it is corrected within the window; error before $\tau$ is not carried in, the free-run validation carries it
\end{itemize}
\fi

\subsection{Identification}\label{sec:aug_closed_loop}
\ifdraft
\begin{itemize}
\item $\theta_{\mathrm{base}}$ is estimated jointly with network and encoder, as in 2026 Eq.~(22); Kessels trains only the network weights (Eq.~(5.12))
\item Training coordinates $\beta$, zero at $\theta^0_{\mathrm{base}}$: nine combinations logarithmic, $m_\Delta$ through \eqref{eq:mdelta_map}; every $\beta$ admissible, so no clamp or penalty (this work, D-229; adapted from Drenth Sec.~4.2)
\item Criterion \eqref{eq:aug_loss}: Eq.~(22) adapted by the loop of Section~\ref{sec:aug_loop} and the encoder of Section~\ref{sec:aug_encoder}; every window sample scored; controller fixed; a closed-loop fit can mask plant error (Section~VI)
\item The baseline/network split is not unique (2026 Sec.~5.2), so $\theta_{\mathrm{base}}$ is not interpretable in the sense of Section~I; Section~IV addresses this (unique to first order only?)
\item Adam, then an unbounded L-BFGS polish (adapted from Drenth Sec.~4.1); checkpoint with the lowest closed-loop free-run error over whole validation records; polish kept only if it lowers that error
\item Initialisation \eqref{eq:aug_init}: $\tilde x$ and $\hat y$ reproduce the baseline, $\bar x$ evolves through a live $g_{\mathrm{aug}}$ (2026 Eq.~(29)); adapted from Sec.~5.4.3 (random added-state rows, no linear bypass); the model is named in Section~\ref{sec:setup}, not here
\end{itemize}
\fi

$\theta_{\mathrm{base}}$ fixed~\cite{hoekstra2026encoder}.}

which are zero at the initial parameters $\theta^0_{\mathrm{base}}$ and keep
every iterate admissible (Section~\ref{sec:params}).
The nine positive parameter combinations $j$ of \eqref{eq:phi} are
$\theta_{\mathrm{base},j}=\theta^0_{\mathrm{base},j}\exp(\beta_j)$,
while $m_\Delta$ can be positive or negative and is bounded
by \eqref{eq:lfr_admissibility}:
[equation \eqref{eq:mdelta_map} moved to Section~\ref{sec:params}]
where $\beta_\Delta$ is the entry of $\beta$ for $m_\Delta$ and
$\gamma\in(0,1)$ provides a safety margin.
We choose the offset $\eta_0$ and scale $s$ so that
$\beta=0$ gives $m_\Delta=m_{\Delta,0}$ and
$\partial m_\Delta/\partial\beta_\Delta=m_{\Delta,0}$.
This matches the logarithmic parameters, where
$\partial\theta_{\mathrm{base},j}/\partial\beta_j
=\theta^0_{\mathrm{base},j}$ at $\beta=0$
(Appendix~\ref{app:lfr-wellposed}).
The initial value must satisfy
$\lvert m_{\Delta,0}\rvert<\gamma(2/L_b)\sqrt{m_{\Sigma,0}J_{\mathrm{eff},0}}$.
The bound in \eqref{eq:lfr_admissibility} holds for
every $\beta$, therefore no clamping or penalty is needed.}
\delmv[M-p8]{IV-C, below}{The parameters
$\vartheta=(\beta,\theta_{\mathrm{aug}},\theta_{\mathrm{enc}})$
are trained to minimise the normalised output error of the
closed-loop simulation, with the

adapted for the closed loop of Section~\ref{sec:aug_loop} and the
encoder described below:
[criterion \eqref{eq:aug_loss} moved below]
for $\tau\le k<\tau+n_f$, where each training window starts at a sample
$\tau\in\mathcal W$ and has length $n_f$, $n_y=3$, and
$\theta_{\mathrm{base}}(\beta)$ gives the baseline parameters.
$W_r=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{y,j}/\sigma_{e,r,j})$ weights axis $j$ of training
record $r$, so that its residual in metres is divided by the standard
deviation $\sigma_{e,r,j}$ of its servo error \eqref{eq:setup_rms}.}

Each simulation window starts\kwtwo{ at a sample $\tau$} from an initial state $\hat x_\tau$\del[own]{,
and $k$ denotes the sample within the window}, but we
measure only the positions of the physical state $\tilde x$.
% NOTATION (2026-10-19, Maarten p8 "tau or k? you normally use k to denote
%   the sample time."): tau = window start, k = sample in the window.
The additional states $\bar x$ are latent\kwtwo{, but we need
their initial values at $\tau$ to simulate each window}.
% (2026-10-23, Dirk): the k sentence placed after the x-bar sentence, so the
%   two sentences on the unknown initial state follow each other.
\add[own]{\kwtwo{Within the window, $k$ denotes the sample.}}
Estimating $\hat x_\tau$ as a separate parameter for each window
would increase the number of parameters as the data
grows~\cite[Sec.~3.1]{beintema2023subnet}.
Following Beintema et al., we use \kwtwo{an encoder network} that estimates $\hat x_\tau$ from
\add[own]{the }past inputs and outputs\add[own]{ $\chi_\tau$}~\cite[Sec.~3.2]{beintema2023subnet}.
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-23): chi_tau named where IV-C introduces the
%   encoder, so (22) does not use it before (23); Section II already
%   introduces the encoder from past inputs and outputs (Dirk 2026-10-23).
keeps the computation per gradient step independent of the record length\add[own]{,}
for \add[own]{a }fixed batch size and window \chg[own]{lengths}{length}~\cite[Sec.~3.1, Eq.~(9)]{beintema2023subnet}.
Using short simulation windows increases the loss function
smoothness~\cite[Sec.~3.1, 4.2]{beintema2023subnet}.

\subsection{Identification}\label{sec:aug_closed_loop}
\ifdraft
\begin{itemize}
\item $\theta_{\mathrm{base}}$ is estimated jointly with network and encoder, as in 2026 Eq.~(22); Kessels trains only the network weights (Eq.~(5.12))
\item Training coordinates $\beta$, zero at $\theta^0_{\mathrm{base}}$: nine combinations logarithmic, $m_\Delta$ through \eqref{eq:mdelta_map}; every $\beta$ admissible, so no clamp or penalty (this work, D-229; adapted from Drenth Sec.~4.2)
\item Criterion \eqref{eq:aug_loss}: Eq.~(22) adapted by the loop of Section~\ref{sec:aug_loop} and the encoder of Section~\ref{sec:aug_encoder}; every window sample scored; controller fixed; a closed-loop fit can mask plant error (Section~VI)
\item The baseline/network split is not unique (2026 Sec.~5.2), so $\theta_{\mathrm{base}}$ is not interpretable in the sense of Section~I; Section~IV addresses this (unique to first order only?)
\item Adam, then an unbounded L-BFGS polish (adapted from Drenth Sec.~4.1); checkpoint with the lowest closed-loop free-run error over whole validation records; polish kept only if it lowers that error
\item Initialisation \eqref{eq:aug_init}: $\tilde x$ and $\hat y$ reproduce the baseline, $\bar x$ evolves through a live $g_{\mathrm{aug}}$ (2026 Eq.~(29)); adapted from Sec.~5.4.3 (random added-state rows, no linear bypass); the model is named in Section~\ref{sec:setup}, not here
\end{itemize}
\fi

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 &\min_{\vartheta}\;V(\vartheta)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal W|\,n_f\,n_y}
 \sum_{\tau\in\mathcal W}\sum_{k=\tau}^{\tau+n_f-1}
 \norm{W_r\bigl(y^{\mathrm n}_{k}-\hat y^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\bigr)}_2^2\quad\text{s.t.}\\
 &\tilde x^{\mathrm n}_{k+1|\tau}
  =f^{\mathrm n}_{\mathrm{base}}\bigl(\theta_{\mathrm{base}}(\beta),
   \tilde x^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau},\hat u^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\bigr)
  +f^{\mathrm n}_{\mathrm{aug}}\bigl(\theta_{\mathrm{aug}},
   \hat x^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau},\hat u^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\bigr),\\
 &\bar x_{k+1|\tau}=g^{\mathrm n}_{\mathrm{aug}}\bigl(\theta_{\mathrm{aug}},
   \hat x^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau},\hat u^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\bigr),\\
 &\hat x^{\mathrm n}_{\tau|\tau}=\psi(\theta_{\mathrm{enc}},\chi_\tau),\quad
  \hat y^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau},\,\hat u^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\text{ from \eqref{eq:aug_cl_step}},
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:aug_loss}
\end{equation}
for $\tau\le k<\tau+n_f$, where each training window starts at a sample
$\tau\in\mathcal W$\add[own]{ of record $r$} and has length $n_f$, $n_y=3$, and
$\theta_{\mathrm{base}}(\beta)$ gives the baseline parameters\add[own]{ (Section~\ref{sec:params})}.

$W_r=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{y,j}/\sigma_{e,r,j})$ weights axis $j$ of \chg[own]{training
record $r$}{record $r$}, so that its residual in metres is divided by the standard
deviation $\sigma_{e,r,j}$ of its servo error\chg[M-mail]{ \eqref{eq:setup_rms}}{ $y_j-r_j$}.

 &\qquad(u^{\mathrm n}_{\tau-n-1})^\top\;\cdots\;(u^{\mathrm n}_{\tau-1})^\top\bigr]^\top,

of Fig.~\ref{fig:aug_structure} at the start of the window,}

\subsection{Identification}\label{sec:aug_closed_loop}
\ifdraft
\begin{itemize}
\item $\theta_{\mathrm{base}}$ is estimated jointly with network and encoder, as in 2026 Eq.~(22); Kessels trains only the network weights (Eq.~(5.12))
\item Training coordinates $\beta$, zero at $\theta^0_{\mathrm{base}}$: nine combinations logarithmic, $m_\Delta$ through \eqref{eq:mdelta_map}; every $\beta$ admissible, so no clamp or penalty (this work, D-229; adapted from Drenth Sec.~4.2)
\item Criterion \eqref{eq:aug_loss}: Eq.~(22) adapted by the loop of Section~\ref{sec:aug_loop} and the encoder of Section~\ref{sec:aug_encoder}; every window sample scored; controller fixed; a closed-loop fit can mask plant error (Section~VI)
\item The baseline/network split is not unique (2026 Sec.~5.2), so $\theta_{\mathrm{base}}$ is not interpretable in the sense of Section~I; Section~IV addresses this (unique to first order only?)
\item Adam, then an unbounded L-BFGS polish (adapted from Drenth Sec.~4.1); checkpoint with the lowest closed-loop free-run error over whole validation records; polish kept only if it lowers that error
\item Initialisation \eqref{eq:aug_init}: $\tilde x$ and $\hat y$ reproduce the baseline, $\bar x$ evolves through a live $g_{\mathrm{aug}}$ (2026 Eq.~(29)); adapted from Sec.~5.4.3 (random added-state rows, no linear bypass); the model is named in Section~\ref{sec:setup}, not here
\end{itemize}
\fi

\subsection{Identification}\label{sec:aug_closed_loop}
\ifdraft
\begin{itemize}
\item $\theta_{\mathrm{base}}$ is estimated jointly with network and encoder, as in 2026 Eq.~(22); Kessels trains only the network weights (Eq.~(5.12))
\item Training coordinates $\beta$, zero at $\theta^0_{\mathrm{base}}$: nine combinations logarithmic, $m_\Delta$ through \eqref{eq:mdelta_map}; every $\beta$ admissible, so no clamp or penalty (this work, D-229; adapted from Drenth Sec.~4.2)
\item Criterion \eqref{eq:aug_loss}: Eq.~(22) adapted by the loop of Section~\ref{sec:aug_loop} and the encoder of Section~\ref{sec:aug_encoder}; every window sample scored; controller fixed; a closed-loop fit can mask plant error (Section~VI)
\item The baseline/network split is not unique (2026 Sec.~5.2), so $\theta_{\mathrm{base}}$ is not interpretable in the sense of Section~I; Section~IV addresses this (unique to first order only?)
\item Adam, then an unbounded L-BFGS polish (adapted from Drenth Sec.~4.1); checkpoint with the lowest closed-loop free-run error over whole validation records; polish kept only if it lowers that error
\item Initialisation \eqref{eq:aug_init}: $\tilde x$ and $\hat y$ reproduce the baseline, $\bar x$ evolves through a live $g_{\mathrm{aug}}$ (2026 Eq.~(29)); adapted from Sec.~5.4.3 (random added-state rows, no linear bypass); the model is named in Section~\ref{sec:setup}, not here

\delmv[M-mail]{III-C}{The optimiser updates $\theta_{\mathrm{base}}$ through training coordinates $\beta\in\R^{10}$,
which are zero at the initial parameters $\theta^0_{\mathrm{base}}$ and keep

$\theta_{\mathrm{base},j}=\theta^0_{\mathrm{base},j}\exp(\beta_j)$,
while $m_\Delta$ can be positive or negative and is bounded
by \eqref{eq:lfr_admissibility}:
[equation \eqref{eq:mdelta_map} moved to Section~\ref{sec:params}]
where $\beta_\Delta$ is the entry of $\beta$ for $m_\Delta$ and
$\gamma\in(0,1)$ provides a safety margin.
We choose the offset $\eta_0$ and scale $s$ so that
$\beta=0$ gives $m_\Delta=m_{\Delta,0}$ and
$\partial m_\Delta/\partial\beta_\Delta=m_{\Delta,0}$.
This matches the logarithmic parameters, where
$\partial\theta_{\mathrm{base},j}/\partial\beta_j
=\theta^0_{\mathrm{base},j}$ at $\beta=0$
(Appendix~\ref{app:lfr-wellposed}).
The initial value must satisfy
$\lvert m_{\Delta,0}\rvert<\gamma(2/L_b)\sqrt{m_{\Sigma,0}J_{\mathrm{eff},0}}$.
The bound in \eqref{eq:lfr_admissibility} holds for
every $\beta$, therefore no clamping or penalty is needed.}

for $\tau\le k<\tau+n_f$, where each training window starts at a sample

$\theta_{\mathrm{base}}(\beta)$ gives the baseline parameters.
$W_r=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{y,j}/\sigma_{e,r,j})$ weights axis $j$ of training
record $r$, so that its residual in metres is divided by the standard

Each simulation window starts\kwtwo{ at a sample $\tau$} from an initial state $\hat x_\tau$\del[own]{,
and $k$ denotes the sample within the window}, but we
measure only the positions of the physical state $\tilde x$.

The additional states $\bar x$ are latent\kwtwo{, but we need
their initial values at $\tau$ to simulate each window}.

%   two sentences on the unknown initial state follow each other.
\add[own]{\kwtwo{Within the window, $k$ denotes the sample.}}
Estimating $\hat x_\tau$ as a separate parameter for each window
would increase the number of parameters as the data
grows~\cite[Sec.~3.1]{beintema2023subnet}.
Following Beintema et al., we use \kwtwo{an encoder network} that estimates $\hat x_\tau$ from
\add[own]{the }past inputs and outputs\add[own]{ $\chi_\tau$}~\cite[Sec.~3.2]{beintema2023subnet}.
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-23): chi_tau named where IV-C introduces the
%   encoder, so (22) does not use it before (23); Section II already
%   introduces the encoder from past inputs and outputs (Dirk 2026-10-23).
keeps the computation per gradient step independent of the record length\add[own]{,}
for \add[own]{a }fixed batch size and window \chg[own]{lengths}{length}~\cite[Sec.~3.1, Eq.~(9)]{beintema2023subnet}.
Using short simulation windows increases the loss function
smoothness~\cite[Sec.~3.1, 4.2]{beintema2023subnet}.

\mv[M-p8]{IV-C start}{\kwtwo{The network parameters $\theta_{\mathrm{aug}}$, the encoder parameters $\theta_{\mathrm{enc}}$ and} $\theta_{\mathrm{base}}$ are jointly estimated,
as in~\cite[Eq.~(22)]{hoekstra2026lfr}\kwtwo{, while the encoder paper keeps

\mv[M-p8]{IV-C start}{The parameters
$\vartheta=(\beta,\theta_{\mathrm{aug}},\theta_{\mathrm{enc}})$
are trained to minimise the normalised output error of the
closed-loop simulation, with the
\chg[own]{controller fixed}{known controller $K_{\mathrm{fb}}$}. We adapt this from~\cite[Eq.~(22)]{hoekstra2026lfr}\del[own]{,
adapted} for the closed loop of Section~\ref{sec:aug_loop} and the
encoder\del[M-mail]{ \kwtwo{described below}}:
% FEEDBACK (Dirk, 2026-10-23): "fixed" -> "known" as in Section II (the
%   controller is not estimated); the double "adapt ... adapted" removed.
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-22; Codex review, Maarten mail forward
%   references): the encoder is motivated above and defined right after
%   (22) (Dirk 2026-10-22).
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 &\min_{\vartheta}\;V(\vartheta)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal W|\,n_f\,n_y}
 \sum_{\tau\in\mathcal W}\sum_{k=\tau}^{\tau+n_f-1}
 \norm{W_r\bigl(y^{\mathrm n}_{k}-\hat y^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\bigr)}_2^2\quad\text{s.t.}\\
 &\tilde x^{\mathrm n}_{k+1|\tau}
  =f^{\mathrm n}_{\mathrm{base}}\bigl(\theta_{\mathrm{base}}(\beta),
   \tilde x^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau},\hat u^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\bigr)
  +f^{\mathrm n}_{\mathrm{aug}}\bigl(\theta_{\mathrm{aug}},
   \hat x^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau},\hat u^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\bigr),\\
 &\bar x_{k+1|\tau}=g^{\mathrm n}_{\mathrm{aug}}\bigl(\theta_{\mathrm{aug}},
   \hat x^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau},\hat u^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\bigr),\\
 &\hat x^{\mathrm n}_{\tau|\tau}=\psi(\theta_{\mathrm{enc}},\chi_\tau),\quad
  \hat y^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau},\,\hat u^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\text{ from \eqref{eq:aug_cl_step}},
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:aug_loss}
\end{equation}
for $\tau\le k<\tau+n_f$, where each training window starts at a sample
$\tau\in\mathcal W$\add[own]{ of record $r$} and has length $n_f$, $n_y=3$, and
$\theta_{\mathrm{base}}(\beta)$ gives the baseline parameters\add[own]{ (Section~\ref{sec:params})}.
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-23; Codex IV-C check, finding 2): ties tau to the
%   record r of W_r (Dirk 2026-10-23).
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-23): first use of "record" in the thesis; D_N
%   (Section II, the estimation set) consists of several records, in
%   Dirk's Section V wording ("The data consist of simulated records"),

% (2026-10-23, Dirk): the record sentence moved up, before the windows
%   paragraph, so "record r" in the where-clause of (22) is defined first.
$W_r=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{y,j}/\sigma_{e,r,j})$ weights axis $j$ of \chg[own]{training
record $r$}{record $r$}, so that its residual in metres is divided by the standard
deviation $\sigma_{e,r,j}$ of its servo error\chg[M-mail]{ \eqref{eq:setup_rms}}{ $y_j-r_j$}.

it can hide errors in the plant model.
We therefore also test the model with a different controller
in Section~\ref{sec:results}.}}
\\
\chg[M-p8]{The encoder uses}{\kwtwo{In \eqref{eq:aug_loss}, the encoder $\psi$ uses}} the samples up to $\tau-1$,
as in~\cite[Eq.~(22e)]{hoekstra2026lfr}:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \hat x^{\mathrm n}_{\tau|\tau}
 &=\psi(\theta_{\mathrm{enc}},\chi_\tau),\\
 \chi_\tau&=\bigl[\,(y^{\mathrm n}_{\tau-n-1})^\top\;\cdots\;(y^{\mathrm n}_{\tau-1})^\top\\
 &\qquad(u^{\mathrm n}_{\tau-n-1})^\top\;\cdots\;(u^{\mathrm n}_{\tau-1})^\top\bigr]^\top,
\end{aligned}
 \label{eq:aug_encoder}
\end{equation}
where \kwtwo{$\hat x^{\mathrm n}_{\tau|\tau}$ is the normalised state $\hat x_\tau$
of Fig.~\ref{fig:aug_structure} at the start of the window,}
% NOTATION (2026-10-19, Maarten p6 on Fig. 3): links the window notation of
%   the text to the loop notation of the figure.
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-23): "the window" meant the simulation window of
%   n_f samples up to here; this is the encoder's past window (Dirk 2026-10-23).
$n+1$ is the number of \add[own]{past }samples \chg[own]{in the window}{used by the encoder},
\add[own]{and }$\chi_\tau\in\R^{6(n+1)}$ stacks the normalised recorded
outputs and inputs as in \eqref{eq:aug_norm}\del[own]{, and $\theta_{\mathrm{enc}}\in\R^{n_{\mathrm{enc}}}$
is the parameter vector of the encoder}.
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-23): theta_enc is introduced before (22) and
%   defined after (24); n_enc is not used elsewhere (Dirk 2026-10-23).
The encoder estimates all $6+n_{\bar x}$ initial states $\hat x_\tau$, 
which includes the measured positions.
We estimate the positions instead of using the measured $y_\tau$ to keep 
the positions consistent with the estimated velocities.
\\
% , and to 
% average out measurement noise over the window.
The encoder uses a linear map with a nonlinear
correction~\cite[Eq.~(8)]{hoekstra2026encoder}:
\begin{equation}
 \psi(\theta_{\mathrm{enc}},\chi_\tau)
 =\begin{bmatrix}W^b\\ W^a\end{bmatrix}\chi_\tau
  +\tilde\psi(\chi_\tau),
 \label{eq:aug_enc_lin}
\end{equation}

%   of the where-clause; the names moved into it. theta^a_enc moved to IV-E,
%   where S1 uses it (theta^b_enc is likewise defined where used, IV-D)
%   (Dirk 2026-10-23).
where $W^b\in\R^{6\times6(n+1)}$ and $W^a\in\R^{n_{\bar x}\times6(n+1)}$ are
the linear maps for the six physical states\add[own]{ $\psi_b$} and the $n_{\bar x}$ additional
states\add[own]{ $\psi_a$}, and $\tilde\psi$ is a neural network.
The encoder parameters $\theta_{\mathrm{enc}}$ are $W^b$, $W^a$ and the
parameters of $\tilde\psi$.

$n_{\bar x}$ outputs $\psi_a$ estimate the additional states.}

\end{itemize}

\subsection{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
% FEEDBACK (Dirk, 2026-10-24): Discussion rewritten with Dirk in the chat, one paragraph per aspect
%   plus limits, from his own sentences (Hoekstra 2026 Sec. 6.3 and 7.4 as model); new: integrators,
%   controller rate (D-265), controller hides overlap, black box against grey box. Numbers from
%   Results/24-10-2026/CSV. Answers M-p15b (separate subsection), M-p15c, M-p15e, M-p15f, Q-p9.
%   The old text is kept below as commented-out source.
%   Marks (2026-10-24, Dirk): black = Dirk's own sentences, red = new or changed words only.
The improvement on the multisine records comes mainly from the
learned absorber mode\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{, which needs both the added states and their PS
initialisation}} (Fig.~\ref{fig:res_frf}\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{, Table~\ref{tab:res_structure}}}).
Without multisine, the final model performs slightly worse than the baseline.
% FEEDBACK (Dirk, 2026-10-24): review: observation first, the integrators as a possible cause only.
\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{Both models stay far above the noise floor on these records.
A possible cause is the free integrators on $X$ and $Y$, which accumulate
small errors.
The training simulates the controller at 4~kHz, while the data are generated
with the controller at 20~kHz.
The augmentation can therefore learn part of this difference as plant
dynamics.}}
\\
OBC reduces the \del[Dirk]{final }combination error compared with the
unconstrained model (69.1 against 83.1\,\%), but the parameters still end up
further from the truth than at their initial values (Table~\ref{tab:res_obc}).
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-24): approved wording changes: separate the recovery explanation and name the comparison.
\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{The constraint holds, but the missing dynamics are not orthogonal to the
parameter directions\chg[own]{ (truth overlap 0.59)}{. Their overlap is 0.59}, so the recovery condition of
Section~\ref{sec:obc_ident} is not met\del[own]{ and the parameters are biased}.
In closed loop, the controller can also hide the effect of this bias on the
output.
\chg[own]{From the correct start and without added states}{Without added states and starting from the true parameters}, OBC does not end closer to
the true values\add[own]{ than the unconstrained model}.}}
With OBC the estimates from the \chg[Dirk]{true and detuned}{\kwtwo{two}} starts are closer together, but still
differ\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{ (31.3 against 36.4\,\%)}}.
% FEEDBACK (Dirk, 2026-10-24): review: observation and possible reason separated (Dirk's two
%   sentences); no uniqueness claim either way (Section IV, M-p15e).
The orthogonality holds only to first order and at $\bar x=0$, and the added
states enter through $f_{\mathrm{aug}}$ without projection.
\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{OBC therefore reduces the dependence on the start, but does not recover
the true values.}}
\\
The final model maintains its accuracy on all extrapolation
records\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{, but}} each record extends beyond the training range in only one
direction (Table~\ref{tab:res_generalisation}).
The black box model performs poorly on its training records and \chg[Dirk]{had not converged}{\kwtwo{did not converge}} within the available budget (Table~\ref{tab:app_bb_search}).
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-24): approved wording change: separate parameter initialisation from controller use.
\chg[own]{It is also randomly initialised and
trained without the controller, while the grey box
starts from the baseline with the controller in the loop}{\kwtwo{The black box model starts from randomly initialised parameters, while the
grey box starts from the physics baseline.
The black box is also trained without the controller}}.
\\
The results are limited to simulation with one seed and the
same controller used to generate the data.
Through the feedback, the recorded input is correlated with the measurement
noise, so the consistency of the \add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{SUBNET }}estimate\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{~\cite{beintema2023subnet}}} is
not shown.
It remains unclear whether the improvements would hold with a different
controller or on measured data.

\subsection{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
% FEEDBACK (Dirk, 2026-10-24): Discussion rewritten with Dirk in the chat, one paragraph per aspect
%   plus limits, from his own sentences (Hoekstra 2026 Sec. 6.3 and 7.4 as model); new: integrators,
%   controller rate (D-265), controller hides overlap, black box against grey box. Numbers from
%   Results/24-10-2026/CSV. Answers M-p15b (separate subsection), M-p15c, M-p15e, M-p15f, Q-p9.
%   The old text is kept below as commented-out source.
%   Marks (2026-10-24, Dirk): black = Dirk's own sentences, red = new or changed words only.
The improvement on the multisine records comes mainly from the
learned absorber mode\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{, which needs both the added states and their PS
initialisation}} (Fig.~\ref{fig:res_frf}\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{, Table~\ref{tab:res_structure}}}).
Without multisine, the final model performs slightly worse than the baseline.
% FEEDBACK (Dirk, 2026-10-24): review: observation first, the integrators as a possible cause only.
\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{Both models stay far above the noise floor on these records.
A possible cause is the free integrators on $X$ and $Y$, which accumulate
small errors.
The training simulates the controller at 4~kHz, while the data are generated
with the controller at 20~kHz.
The augmentation can therefore learn part of this difference as plant
dynamics.}}
\\
OBC reduces the \del[Dirk]{final }combination error compared with the
unconstrained model (69.1 against 83.1\,\%), but the parameters still end up
further from the truth than at their initial values (Table~\ref{tab:res_obc}).
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-24): approved wording changes: separate the recovery explanation and name the comparison.
\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{The constraint holds, but the missing dynamics are not orthogonal to the
parameter directions\chg[own]{ (truth overlap 0.59)}{. Their overlap is 0.59}, so the recovery condition of
Section~\ref{sec:obc_ident} is not met\del[own]{ and the parameters are biased}.
In closed loop, the controller can also hide the effect of this bias on the
output.
\chg[own]{From the correct start and without added states}{Without added states and starting from the true parameters}, OBC does not end closer to
the true values\add[own]{ than the unconstrained model}.}}
With OBC the estimates from the \chg[Dirk]{true and detuned}{\kwtwo{two}} starts are closer together, but still
differ\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{ (31.3 against 36.4\,\%)}}.
% FEEDBACK (Dirk, 2026-10-24): review: observation and possible reason separated (Dirk's two
%   sentences); no uniqueness claim either way (Section IV, M-p15e).
The orthogonality holds only to first order and at $\bar x=0$, and the added
states enter through $f_{\mathrm{aug}}$ without projection.
\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{OBC therefore reduces the dependence on the start, but does not recover
the true values.}}
\\
The final model maintains its accuracy on all extrapolation
records\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{, but}} each record extends beyond the training range in only one
direction (Table~\ref{tab:res_generalisation}).
The black box model performs poorly on its training records and \chg[Dirk]{had not converged}{\kwtwo{did not converge}} within the available budget (Table~\ref{tab:app_bb_search}).
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-24): approved wording change: separate parameter initialisation from controller use.
\chg[own]{It is also randomly initialised and
trained without the controller, while the grey box
starts from the baseline with the controller in the loop}{\kwtwo{The black box model starts from randomly initialised parameters, while the
grey box starts from the physics baseline.
The black box is also trained without the controller}}.
\\
The results are limited to simulation with one seed and the
same controller used to generate the data.
Through the feedback, the recorded input is correlated with the measurement
noise, so the consistency of the \add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{SUBNET }}estimate\add[Dirk]{\kwtwo{~\cite{beintema2023subnet}}} is
not shown.
It remains unclear whether the improvements would hold with a different
controller or on measured data.

\subsection{Black-box model}\label{app:setup_bb}
% Sources: beintema2023subnet; scripts/gantry/blackbox-cl-trainable (train_bb_clmap.py), thesis_r8_grid.conf.
\ifdraft
\begin{itemize}
\item The SUBNET model of the closed loop, from reference and injected force to servo error, with its encoder
\end{itemize}
\fi
The black box of Section~\ref{sec:setup_models} is
\begin{equation}
 x^{\mathrm{bb}}_{k+1}=f_{\mathrm{bb}}\bigl(\theta_{\mathrm{bb}},x^{\mathrm{bb}}_k,r_k,u^{\mathrm{ms}}_k\bigr),\quad
 \hat y_k=r_k+h_{\mathrm{bb}}\bigl(\theta_{\mathrm{bb}},x^{\mathrm{bb}}_k\bigr),
 \label{eq:setup_bb}
\end{equation}
where $x^{\mathrm{bb}}_k\in\R^{n_x}$ and an encoder estimates
$x^{\mathrm{bb}}$ at the window start from past inputs and servo errors, as
in~\cite{beintema2023subnet}.
Its settings are the black-box rows of Table~\ref{tab:hyper}.

\subsection{Added-state initialisation}\label{sec:aug_ps2}
\ifdraft
\begin{itemize}
\item Problem: the start \eqref{eq:aug_init} gives $\tilde x$ a model ($f_{\mathrm{base}}$, $W^b$, output) and $\bar x$ none (random $W^a$, random added-state rows of $\phi_{\mathrm{aug}}$); $V$ scores only the output and $f_{\mathrm{aug}}$ can lower the same error statically, so training can leave the omitted dynamics out of $\bar x$ (Venkatraman Sec.~2.1; Section~VI tests it)
\item PS is this work's, adapted from two-stage regression (Hefny Sec.~2) and its use before BPTT (Downey Sec.~4.2); it gives $\bar x$ a start from data, as $W^b$ gives $\tilde x$ one from the baseline
\item S1: a decoder on $\psi_a$ predicts the current model's residual over $\tau$ to $\tau+H-1$; the minimiser is the conditional mean, so $\bar x_{\tau|\tau}$ becomes a predictive state; trains $\theta_{\mathrm p}$, $\theta^a_{\mathrm{enc}}$ only, one update after every update of $V$
\item Stopping rule: $\nu$ on calibration windows ends S1 (plateau or cap) and decides whether S2 runs
\item S2: once, one-step regression of $g^{\mathrm n}_{\mathrm{aug}}$ on frozen encoder pairs with the recorded input, which equals the loop input when the encoder reproduces $y_{k_i}$; overlapping windows (?)
\item Hand-over: decoder discarded, \eqref{eq:aug_loss} continues from $\vartheta_{\mathrm{PS}}$; deployed model, criterion and selection unchanged; $\bar x$ latent; $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{PS}}$ named
\end{itemize}
\fi

\kwtwo{PS has \chg[own]{three}{two} stages, each with its own \chg[own]{optimisation problem}{cost function}.
\chg[own]{In S1,}{In the first stage (S1),} \chg[own]{\mbox{\eqref{eq:aug_loss}} is minimised as before, and after each of its

\subsection{Added-state initialisation}\label{sec:aug_ps2}
\ifdraft
\begin{itemize}
\item Problem: the start \eqref{eq:aug_init} gives $\tilde x$ a model ($f_{\mathrm{base}}$, $W^b$, output) and $\bar x$ none (random $W^a$, random added-state rows of $\phi_{\mathrm{aug}}$); $V$ scores only the output and $f_{\mathrm{aug}}$ can lower the same error statically, so training can leave the omitted dynamics out of $\bar x$ (Venkatraman Sec.~2.1; Section~VI tests it)
\item PS is this work's, adapted from two-stage regression (Hefny Sec.~2) and its use before BPTT (Downey Sec.~4.2); it gives $\bar x$ a start from data, as $W^b$ gives $\tilde x$ one from the baseline
\item S1: a decoder on $\psi_a$ predicts the current model's residual over $\tau$ to $\tau+H-1$; the minimiser is the conditional mean, so $\bar x_{\tau|\tau}$ becomes a predictive state; trains $\theta_{\mathrm p}$, $\theta^a_{\mathrm{enc}}$ only, one update after every update of $V$
\item Stopping rule: $\nu$ on calibration windows ends S1 (plateau or cap) and decides whether S2 runs
\item S2: once, one-step regression of $g^{\mathrm n}_{\mathrm{aug}}$ on frozen encoder pairs with the recorded input, which equals the loop input when the encoder reproduces $y_{k_i}$; overlapping windows (?)
\item Hand-over: decoder discarded, \eqref{eq:aug_loss} continues from $\vartheta_{\mathrm{PS}}$; deployed model, criterion and selection unchanged; $\bar x$ latent; $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{PS}}$ named
\end{itemize}
\fi

\delmv[Dirk]{A.2}{A linear fractional representation (LFR) is introduced to separate this rational scheduling dependence exactly, with an LTI part whose
matrices do not depend on $Y$.

with the scheduling being connected in feedback
with $G$ (Fig.~\mbox{\ref{fig:lfr}}) \mbox{\cite{drenth2026lpvlfr,hoekstra2026lfr}}.
Substituting \mbox{\eqref{eq:Msplit}} into \mbox{\eqref{eq:eom}} gives (7).
Here $Y$ only enters through $Y\ddot q$ and $Y^2\ddot q$,
with $Y^2\ddot q=Y(Y\ddot q)$. This lets us apply the same scheduling variable twice
instead of introducing a second scheduling variable $Y^2$ (8),
with $a_1=Y\ddot q$ and $a_2=Y^2\ddot q$.
We treat $a_1$ and $a_2$ as independent signals, so (7) becomes (9),
which contains no $Y$.
This is allowed, because the Delta-block below imposes
$a_1=Y\ddot q$ and $a_2=Ya_1$ again.
The latent variables are $z=[\ddot q^\top\;a_1^\top]^\top$ and $w=[a_1^\top\;a_2^\top]^\top$,
with the Delta-block mapping $z$ to $w$ (10).
We write the LTI part $G$ of the LFR in continuous time, adapting the
discrete-time block structure of~\mbox{\cite[Eq.~(2)]{drenth2026lpvlfr}} (11),
where $\tilde x=[q^\top\;\dot q^\top]^\top$ is the state and $q$ the output.
The first block row is the state equation, with $\ddot q$ obtained from
(9) by multiplying with $M_0^{-1}$.
For the blocks of $G$, see Appendix~\mbox{\ref{app:lfr-details}}.
Conversely, closing the algebraic loop with (10) results in
$a_1=Y\ddot q$ and $a_2=Y^2\ddot q$, which turns (9) back
into \mbox{\eqref{eq:eom}}. The LFR is therefore an exact realisation of the baseline.
The LFR is well posed if the algebraic loop has a unique solution for
every $Y$ \mbox{\cite[Def.~1]{drenth2026lpvlfr}}.}

\begin{itemize}

\item Training coordinates $\beta$, zero at $\theta^0_{\mathrm{base}}$: nine combinations logarithmic, $m_\Delta$ through \eqref{eq:mdelta_map}; every $\beta$ admissible, so no clamp or penalty (this work, D-229; adapted from Drenth Sec.~4.2)

\item Adam, then an unbounded L-BFGS polish (adapted from Drenth Sec.~4.1); checkpoint with the lowest closed-loop free-run error over whole validation records; polish kept only if it lowers that error
\item Initialisation \eqref{eq:aug_init}: $\tilde x$ and $\hat y$ reproduce the baseline, $\bar x$ evolves through a live $g_{\mathrm{aug}}$ (2026 Eq.~(29)); adapted from Sec.~5.4.3 (random added-state rows, no linear bypass); the model is named in Section~\ref{sec:setup}, not here
\end{itemize}
\fi

measure only the positions of the physical state $\tilde x$.
% NOTATION (2026-10-19, Maarten p8 "tau or k? you normally use k to denote
%   the sample time."): tau = window start, k = sample in the window.
The additional states $\bar x$ are latent\kwtwo{, but we need
their initial values at $\tau$ to simulate each window}.
% (2026-10-23, Dirk): the k sentence placed after the x-bar sentence, so the
%   two sentences on the unknown initial state follow each other.
\add[own]{\kwtwo{Within the window, $k$ denotes the sample.}}
Estimating $\hat x_\tau$ as a separate parameter for each window
would increase the number of parameters as the data
grows~\cite[Sec.~3.1]{beintema2023subnet}.
Following Beintema et al., we use \kwtwo{an encoder network} that estimates $\hat x_\tau$ from
\add[own]{the }past inputs and outputs\add[own]{ $\chi_\tau$}~\cite[Sec.~3.2]{beintema2023subnet}.
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-23): chi_tau named where IV-C introduces the
%   encoder, so (22) does not use it before (23); Section II already
%   introduces the encoder from past inputs and outputs (Dirk 2026-10-23).
keeps the computation per gradient step independent of the record length\add[own]{,}
for \add[own]{a }fixed batch size and window \chg[own]{lengths}{length}~\cite[Sec.~3.1, Eq.~(9)]{beintema2023subnet}.
Using short simulation windows increases the loss function
smoothness~\cite[Sec.~3.1, 4.2]{beintema2023subnet}.
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-23; Codex math check, finding 11): Sec. 4.2 added,
%   where Beintema shows it (Theorem 9, PDF p8); Sec. 3.1 (PDF p4) states
%   it. No mark inside \cite (a [tag] would end its optional argument).
\\
% RESTRUCTURE (2026-10-19, agreed with Dirk): IV-C order is what (P1), why windows and an encoder (P2),
%   the problem with the encoder inside it (P3, Jan41), encoder details (P4), why closed loop (P5),
%   window start (P6), non-uniqueness, optimiser.
% RESTRUCTURE (2026-10-19, Maarten p8): joint estimation and the criterion moved here, after the encoder they use.
\mv[M-p8]{IV-C start}{\kwtwo{The network parameters $\theta_{\mathrm{aug}}$, the encoder parameters $\theta_{\mathrm{enc}}$ and} $\theta_{\mathrm{base}}$ are jointly estimated,
as in~\cite[Eq.~(22)]{hoekstra2026lfr}\kwtwo{, while the encoder paper keeps
$\theta_{\mathrm{base}}$ fixed~\cite[footnote~1]{hoekstra2026encoder}}.}
\mv[M-p8]{IV-C start}{The parameters
$\vartheta=(\beta,\theta_{\mathrm{aug}},\theta_{\mathrm{enc}})$
are trained to minimise the normalised output error of the
closed-loop simulation, with the
\chg[own]{controller fixed}{known controller $K_{\mathrm{fb}}$}. We adapt this from~\cite[Eq.~(22)]{hoekstra2026lfr}\del[own]{,
adapted} for the closed loop of Section~\ref{sec:aug_loop} and the
encoder\del[M-mail]{ \kwtwo{described below}}:
% FEEDBACK (Dirk, 2026-10-23): "fixed" -> "known" as in Section II (the
%   controller is not estimated); the double "adapt ... adapted" removed.
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-22; Codex review, Maarten mail forward
%   references): the encoder is motivated above and defined right after
%   (22) (Dirk 2026-10-22).
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 &\min_{\vartheta}\;V(\vartheta)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal W|\,n_f\,n_y}
 \sum_{\tau\in\mathcal W}\sum_{k=\tau}^{\tau+n_f-1}
 \norm{W_r\bigl(y^{\mathrm n}_{k}-\hat y^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\bigr)}_2^2\quad\text{s.t.}\\
 &\tilde x^{\mathrm n}_{k+1|\tau}
  =f^{\mathrm n}_{\mathrm{base}}\bigl(\theta_{\mathrm{base}}(\beta),
   \tilde x^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau},\hat u^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\bigr)
  +f^{\mathrm n}_{\mathrm{aug}}\bigl(\theta_{\mathrm{aug}},
   \hat x^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau},\hat u^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\bigr),\\
 &\bar x_{k+1|\tau}=g^{\mathrm n}_{\mathrm{aug}}\bigl(\theta_{\mathrm{aug}},
   \hat x^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau},\hat u^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\bigr),\\
 &\hat x^{\mathrm n}_{\tau|\tau}=\psi(\theta_{\mathrm{enc}},\chi_\tau),\quad
  \hat y^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau},\,\hat u^{\mathrm n}_{k|\tau}\text{ from \eqref{eq:aug_cl_step}},
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:aug_loss}
\end{equation}
for $\tau\le k<\tau+n_f$, where each training window starts at a sample
$\tau\in\mathcal W$\add[own]{ of record $r$} and has length $n_f$, $n_y=3$, and
$\theta_{\mathrm{base}}(\beta)$ gives the baseline parameters\add[own]{ (Section~\ref{sec:params})}.
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-23; Codex IV-C check, finding 2): ties tau to the
%   record r of W_r (Dirk 2026-10-23).
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-23): first use of "record" in the thesis; D_N
%   (Section II, the estimation set) consists of several records, in
%   Dirk's Section V wording ("The data consist of simulated records"),
%   as its own sentence before W_r; Dirk's W_r sentence kept with
%   "training record r" -> "record r" (convention A, Dirk 2026-10-23).
% (2026-10-23, Dirk): the record sentence moved up, before the windows
%   paragraph, so "record r" in the where-clause of (22) is defined first.
$W_r=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{y,j}/\sigma_{e,r,j})$ weights axis $j$ of \chg[own]{training
record $r$}{record $r$}, so that its residual in metres is divided by the standard
deviation $\sigma_{e,r,j}$ of its servo error\chg[M-mail]{ \eqref{eq:setup_rms}}{ $y_j-r_j$}.
\todo{might have to move to discussion if i dont add it. Since the controller corrects part of the output error,
it can hide errors in the plant model.
We therefore also test the model with a different controller
in Section~\ref{sec:results}.}}
\\
\chg[M-p8]{The encoder uses}{\kwtwo{In \eqref{eq:aug_loss}, the encoder $\psi$ uses}} the samples up to $\tau-1$,
as in~\cite[Eq.~(22e)]{hoekstra2026lfr}:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \hat x^{\mathrm n}_{\tau|\tau}
 &=\psi(\theta_{\mathrm{enc}},\chi_\tau),\\
 \chi_\tau&=\bigl[\,(y^{\mathrm n}_{\tau-n-1})^\top\;\cdots\;(y^{\mathrm n}_{\tau-1})^\top\\
 &\qquad(u^{\mathrm n}_{\tau-n-1})^\top\;\cdots\;(u^{\mathrm n}_{\tau-1})^\top\bigr]^\top,
\end{aligned}
 \label{eq:aug_encoder}
\end{equation}
where \kwtwo{$\hat x^{\mathrm n}_{\tau|\tau}$ is the normalised state $\hat x_\tau$
of Fig.~\ref{fig:aug_structure} at the start of the window,}
% NOTATION (2026-10-19, Maarten p6 on Fig. 3): links the window notation of
%   the text to the loop notation of the figure.
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-23): "the window" meant the simulation window of
%   n_f samples up to here; this is the encoder's past window (Dirk 2026-10-23).
$n+1$ is the number of \add[own]{past }samples \chg[own]{in the window}{used by the encoder},
\add[own]{and }$\chi_\tau\in\R^{6(n+1)}$ stacks the normalised recorded
outputs and inputs as in \eqref{eq:aug_norm}\del[own]{, and $\theta_{\mathrm{enc}}\in\R^{n_{\mathrm{enc}}}$
is the parameter vector of the encoder}.
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-23): theta_enc is introduced before (22) and
%   defined after (24); n_enc is not used elsewhere (Dirk 2026-10-23).
The encoder estimates all $6+n_{\bar x}$ initial states $\hat x_\tau$, 
which includes the measured positions.
We estimate the positions instead of using the measured $y_\tau$ to keep 
the positions consistent with the estimated velocities.
\\
% , and to 
% average out measurement noise over the window.
The encoder uses a linear map with a nonlinear
correction~\cite[Eq.~(8)]{hoekstra2026encoder}:
\begin{equation}
 \psi(\theta_{\mathrm{enc}},\chi_\tau)
 =\begin{bmatrix}W^b\\ W^a\end{bmatrix}\chi_\tau
  +\tilde\psi(\chi_\tau),
 \label{eq:aug_enc_lin}
\end{equation}
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-23): the psi_b/psi_a sentence repeated the split
%   of the where-clause; the names moved into it. theta^a_enc moved to IV-E,
%   where S1 uses it (theta^b_enc is likewise defined where used, IV-D)
%   (Dirk 2026-10-23).
where $W^b\in\R^{6\times6(n+1)}$ and $W^a\in\R^{n_{\bar x}\times6(n+1)}$ are
the linear maps for the six physical states\add[own]{ $\psi_b$} and the $n_{\bar x}$ additional
states\add[own]{ $\psi_a$}, and $\tilde\psi$ is a neural network.
The encoder parameters $\theta_{\mathrm{enc}}$ are $W^b$, $W^a$ and the
parameters of $\tilde\psi$.
\del[own]{The first six outputs $\psi_b$ estimate the physical states and the remaining
$n_{\bar x}$ outputs $\psi_a$ estimate the additional states.}
\delmv[own]{IV-E}{We use $\theta^a_{\mathrm{enc}}$ for the parameters
that affect only $\psi_a$: $W^a$ and the additional-state
rows of the output layer of $\tilde\psi$.}

We move the dependence out of the LTI part $G$ and into a Delta-block $\Dsch(Y)$,
with the scheduling being connected in feedback
with $G$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:lfr}) \cite{drenth2026lpvlfr,hoekstra2026lfr}.}
\begin{figure}[!ht]
  \centering
  \input{figures/lfr_loop}
  \caption{Self-scheduled baseline interconnection. The Delta-block closes
  the latent variables of $G$ through $w=\Dsch(Y)z$, with
  $\Dsch(Y)=YI_6$ and $Y$ a component of the state.}
  % FEEDBACK: caption taken out of its \todo (Js42); no marks in captions.
  % Moved from III-B (2026-10-22, Dirk).
  \label{fig:lfr}
\end{figure}
\mv[Dirk]{III-B}{Substituting \eqref{eq:Msplit} into \eqref{eq:eom} gives}
\begin{equation}
  M_0\ddot q+YM_1\ddot q+Y^2M_2\ddot q=u-C\dot q-Kq.
  \label{eq:lfr_mass_factorization}
\end{equation}
\mv[Dirk]{III-B}{Here $Y$ only enters through $Y\ddot q$ and $Y^2\ddot q$,
with $Y^2\ddot q=Y(Y\ddot q)$. This lets us apply the same scheduling variable twice
instead of introducing a second scheduling variable $Y^2$,}
\begin{equation}
  \ddot q\xrightarrow{\;Y\;}a_1\xrightarrow{\;Y\;}a_2,
  \label{eq:lfr_chain}
\end{equation}
\mv[Dirk]{III-B}{with $a_1=Y\ddot q$ and $a_2=Y^2\ddot q$.
We treat $a_1$ and $a_2$ as independent signals, so \eqref{eq:lfr_mass_factorization}
becomes}
\begin{equation}
  M_0\ddot q+M_1a_1+M_2a_2=u-C\dot q-Kq,
  \label{eq:lfr_constant}
\end{equation}
\mv[Dirk]{III-B}{which contains no $Y$.
This is allowed, because the Delta-block below imposes
$a_1=Y\ddot q$ and $a_2=Ya_1$ again.
The latent variables are $z=[\ddot q^\top\;a_1^\top]^\top$ and $w=[a_1^\top\;a_2^\top]^\top$,
with the Delta-block mapping $z$ to $w$,}
\begin{equation}
  w=\begin{bmatrix}a_1\\a_2\end{bmatrix}
   =\begin{bmatrix}Y\ddot q\\Ya_1\end{bmatrix}
   =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}YI_3&0\\0&YI_3\end{bmatrix}}_{\Dsch(Y)=YI_6}
    \begin{bmatrix}\ddot q\\a_1\end{bmatrix}
   =\Dsch(Y)z.
  \label{eq:delta}
\end{equation}
\mv[Dirk]{III-B}{We write the LTI part $G$ of the LFR in continuous time, adapting the
discrete-time block structure of~\cite[Eq.~(2)]{drenth2026lpvlfr}:}
\todo{Check this}
\begin{equation}
  \begin{bmatrix}\dot{\tilde x}\\ z\\ q\end{bmatrix}
  =G\begin{bmatrix}\tilde x\\ w\\ u\end{bmatrix},
  \label{eq:lfr_G}
\end{equation}
\mv[Dirk]{III-B}{where $\tilde x=[q^\top\;\dot q^\top]^\top$ is the state and $q$ the output.
The first block row is the state equation, with $\ddot q$ obtained from
\eqref{eq:lfr_constant} by multiplying with $M_0^{-1}$.}
% REVNOTE closed (2026-10-22, Dirk): "This was not clear earlier for
%   Maarten ..." is answered by the explicit state equation eq:base_ss in
%   III-B; III-C will cite it for Maarten v2 p5.
\mv[Dirk]{III-B}{Conversely, closing the algebraic loop with \eqref{eq:delta} results in
$a_1=Y\ddot q$ and $a_2=Y^2\ddot q$, which turns \eqref{eq:lfr_constant} back
into \eqref{eq:eom}. The LFR is therefore an exact realisation of the baseline.
The LFR is well posed if the algebraic loop has a unique solution for
every $Y$ \cite[Def.~1]{drenth2026lpvlfr}.}

sections/99_appendix.tex:325 | draft material | cite Thm.~6
\begin{wip}
\todo{Remarks cut from Section~II-B; keep here or drop?}
\begin{itemize}
\item $Y^2$ is realised by repeating $Y$, not as a second scheduling variable $p_2=Y^2$, which would admit pairs with $p_2\neq Y^2$; extra scheduling variables cause overbounding in controller synthesis \cite{drenth2026lpvlfr}
\item The scheduling map is a known selection of the state ($Y=q_3$), not a learned map as in the self-scheduled models of \cite{drenth2026lpvlfr}
\item The exact condition $\det M(Y)\neq0$ replaces the sufficient condition of \cite[Thm.~6]{drenth2026lpvlfr}, which needs a scheduling set in the unit ball and $\rho(D_{zw})<1$
\item Drenth's Def.~1 is stated in discrete time but constrains only the algebraic loop equation, so it applies unchanged in continuous time
\end{itemize}
\end{wip}

\begin{itemize}

\item The concrete digital-twin use case is to evaluate relevant ASMPT motion and a changed controller before deployment on the machine
\item The physics model exposes masses, stiffnesses, damping, and coupling, but omits position-dependent flexible dynamics that matter for prediction
\item A black-box model offers flexibility but weakens extrapolation arguments and removes parameters useful for control design, digital twins, and health monitoring
\item Grey-box dynamic augmentation is the target compromise: preserve the baseline and learn only the missing state dynamics \cite{hoekstra2026lfr}
\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

White-box models are attractive because they reflect the physics of the
system, which makes them interpretable.
First-principles (FP) models are a specific type of white-box model,
derived from physical laws and described by quantities such as mass,
stiffness, and damping.
However, purely physics-based models do not always capture all behaviour
needed for accurate prediction across the operating range
\cite{willard2020integrating}.
More accurate FP models can be developed, but this is labour-intensive
\cite{hoekstra2026lfr}.

The actuator forces are defined as
$\uact=[F_{X1}\;F_{X2}\;F_Y]^\top$ and the measured positions
$\qact=[X_1\;X_2\;Y]^\top$.
Here $F_{X1}$, $F_{X2}$ and $F_Y$ are the forces and
$X_1$, $X_2$ and $Y$ the measured positions of the
\chg[Dirk]{two X actuators and the Y actuator}{two X and the Y actuators}%
\add[Q17]{\kwtwo{, each from a linear encoder~\cite{garcia2013model}}}.
% FEEDBACK v1 (2026-10-21): Q17 ("add location of encoders"): Garcia Sec.
%   2.1 (PDF p2), each actuator has a linear encoder that measures its
%   position. Js22 ("positions of what? the stages?"): no change, "of the
%   two X actuators and the Y actuator" is Garcia's wording (Sec. 2.2, PDF
%   p3: (X1, X2, Y) are the measured positions of the actuators)
%   (Dirk 2026-10-21).
\\
The system to be identified is the gantry system
described \chg{as,}{by}
\begin{equation}
  \dot x(t)=f\bigl(x(t),\uact(t)\bigr),\qquad y_k=\qact(kT_s)+v_k,
  \label{eq:system}
\end{equation}
% where the \kw{state $x$ is unknown, except that it contains the actuator
% positions $\qact$}, $y_k$ are the measured positions at sample $k$ with
% sampling time $T_s$, and $v_k$ is zero-mean, coloured measurement noise.
% The state-transition function $f$ is unknown.
where the \chg[own]{\kw{state $x$ is unknown, except that it contains the actuator
positions $\qact$}}{state $x$ contains the actuator positions $\qact$}, $y_k$ are the measured positions at sample $k$ with
sampling time $T_s$, and $v_k$ is zero-mean, coloured measurement noise.
The \chg[own]{state-transition function $f$ is}{function $f$ and the
dimension of $x$ are} unknown.
The system runs in closed loop with an assumed known
linear time-invariant feedback controller\del[M-p3]{ (Section~\ref{sec:aug_loop})},
which gives the data set $\mathcal D_N=\{u_{\mathrm{act},k},y_k\}_{k=1}^N$.
% \add[M-p3]{The controller computes the actuator forces from the reference
% $r_k$ and the measured positions, and a feedforward $u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k$ is
% added (Fig.~\ref{fig:system_loop}):}
\add[M-p3]{The controller computes the actuator forces from the
error between the reference $r_k$ and the measured positions $y_k$,
and a feedforward $u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k$ is added (Fig.~\ref{fig:system_loop}):}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 x^{\mathrm{fb}}_{k+1}&=A_{\mathrm{fb}}x^{\mathrm{fb}}_k+B_{\mathrm{fb}}(r_k-y_k),\\
 u_{\mathrm{act},k}&=C_{\mathrm{fb}}x^{\mathrm{fb}}_k+D_{\mathrm{fb}}(r_k-y_k)+u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k,
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:system_loop}
\end{equation}
\mv[M-p3]{IV-B}{where $(A_{\mathrm{fb}},B_{\mathrm{fb}},C_{\mathrm{fb}},D_{\mathrm{fb}})$
are the state-space matrices of the controller\add[own]{ $K_{\mathrm{fb}}$}\add[M-p3]{, with state
$x^{\mathrm{fb}}$,} discretised
with sampling time $T_s$\add[own]{\kwtwo{, and the actuator forces are held
constant between samples, $\uact(t)=u_{\mathrm{act},k}$ for
$kT_s\le t<(k+1)T_s$}}.
% FEEDBACK (own, 2026-10-21): the hold links the continuous-time
%   eq:system to the discrete eq:system_loop; Section II states the
%   assumptions at T_s that Section IV implements (RK4 with the input held,
%   K_1 at T_s); the data's deviations are named in Section V. Checked by
%   the second-opinion session sec2-rate-review against Clean/gantry_dynamic
%   and the Simulink model (Dirk 2026-10-21).
Both $r_k$ and $u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k$ are in actuator coordinates.}
% \add[M-p3]{The noise $v_k$ is independent of $r$ and
% $u^{\mathrm{ff}}$\add[M-p3]{\kwtwo{, but through the feedback it is
% correlated with $u_{\mathrm{act}}$}}.}
\add[M-p3]{The noise $v$ is independent of $r$ and $u^{\mathrm{ff}}$.
The force $u_{\mathrm{act}}$ is correlated with $v$, because the
controller computes it from $y$.}

\\
We use the lumped-parameter model of Fig.~\ref{fig:gantry_system} as our
physics-based baseline model of \eqref{eq:system}.
This model does not capture all dynamics of the system.
We identify these missing dynamics from $\mathcal D_N$ and augment the
baseline with learned components and additional
states~\cite{hoekstra2026lfr}.
% \mv[Jan7]{III intro}{A correction to the states of the baseline model alone is 
% not sufficient,
% \kwtwo{because missing dynamics need states the baseline does not 
% have\del[M-mail]{
% (Section~\ref{sec:aug_structure})},}
% so additional states are introduced.
\\
The goal is to estimate the \kw{physical and learned parameters} of the
augmented model from $\mathcal D_N$, such that it captures the missing
dynamics and accurately predicts the system, while the identifiable
combinations of the physical parameters are estimated uniquely.
% \mv[Jan23]{IV-C}{The model is trained using short windows of the
% closed-loop data, where each window is simulated with
% \chg[own]{the known controller}{the controller $K_{\mathrm{fb}}$}.
% The initial states are estimated by \chg[Q37]{an encoder}{an encoder network}, 
% including the additional states.}
% \add[M-p7]{\kwtwo{This is the SUBNET method of Beintema et
% al.~\cite{beintema2023subnet}: the encoder estimates each initial state
% from past inputs and outputs and is trained jointly with the model.}}
We use the SUBNET method of Beintema et
al.~\cite{beintema2023subnet} to train the model on short windows of
$\mathcal D_N$, where each window is simulated with the controller
$K_{\mathrm{fb}}$.
The initial states are estimated by an encoder network from past inputs and outputs.

The actuator forces are defined as
$\uact=[F_{X1}\;F_{X2}\;F_Y]^\top$ and the measured positions
$\qact=[X_1\;X_2\;Y]^\top$.
Here $F_{X1}$, $F_{X2}$ and $F_Y$ are the forces and
$X_1$, $X_2$ and $Y$ the measured positions of the
\chg[Dirk]{two X actuators and the Y actuator}{two X and the Y actuators}%
\add[Q17]{\kwtwo{, each from a linear encoder~\cite{garcia2013model}}}.
% FEEDBACK v1 (2026-10-21): Q17 ("add location of encoders"): Garcia Sec.

The system to be identified is the gantry system
described \chg{as,}{by}
\begin{equation}
  \dot x(t)=f\bigl(x(t),\uact(t)\bigr),\qquad y_k=\qact(kT_s)+v_k,
  \label{eq:system}
\end{equation}
% where the \kw{state $x$ is unknown, except that it contains the actuator
% positions $\qact$}, $y_k$ are the measured positions at sample $k$ with
% sampling time $T_s$, and $v_k$ is zero-mean, coloured measurement noise.
% The state-transition function $f$ is unknown.
where the \chg[own]{\kw{state $x$ is unknown, except that it contains the actuator
positions $\qact$}}{state $x$ contains the actuator positions $\qact$}, $y_k$ are the measured positions at sample $k$ with
sampling time $T_s$, and $v_k$ is zero-mean, coloured measurement noise.
The \chg[own]{state-transition function $f$ is}{function $f$ and the
dimension of $x$ are} unknown.
The system runs in closed loop with an assumed known
linear time-invariant feedback controller\del[M-p3]{ (Section~\ref{sec:aug_loop})},
which gives the data set $\mathcal D_N=\{u_{\mathrm{act},k},y_k\}_{k=1}^N$.
% \add[M-p3]{The controller computes the actuator forces from the reference
% $r_k$ and the measured positions, and a feedforward $u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k$ is
% added (Fig.~\ref{fig:system_loop}):}
\add[M-p3]{The controller computes the actuator forces from the
error between the reference $r_k$ and the measured positions $y_k$,
and a feedforward $u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k$ is added (Fig.~\ref{fig:system_loop}):}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 x^{\mathrm{fb}}_{k+1}&=A_{\mathrm{fb}}x^{\mathrm{fb}}_k+B_{\mathrm{fb}}(r_k-y_k),\\
 u_{\mathrm{act},k}&=C_{\mathrm{fb}}x^{\mathrm{fb}}_k+D_{\mathrm{fb}}(r_k-y_k)+u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k,
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:system_loop}
\end{equation}
\mv[M-p3]{IV-B}{where $(A_{\mathrm{fb}},B_{\mathrm{fb}},C_{\mathrm{fb}},D_{\mathrm{fb}})$
are the state-space matrices of the controller\add[own]{ $K_{\mathrm{fb}}$}\add[M-p3]{, with state
$x^{\mathrm{fb}}$,} discretised
with sampling time $T_s$\add[own]{\kwtwo{, and the actuator forces are held
constant between samples, $\uact(t)=u_{\mathrm{act},k}$ for
$kT_s\le t<(k+1)T_s$}}.

Both $r_k$ and $u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k$ are in actuator coordinates.}

\add[M-p3]{The noise $v$ is independent of $r$ and $u^{\mathrm{ff}}$.
The force $u_{\mathrm{act}}$ is correlated with $v$, because the
controller computes it from $y$.}

We use the lumped-parameter model of Fig.~\ref{fig:gantry_system} as our
physics-based baseline model of \eqref{eq:system}.
This model does not capture all dynamics of the system.
We identify these missing dynamics from $\mathcal D_N$ and augment the
baseline with learned components and additional
states~\cite{hoekstra2026lfr}.
% \mv[Jan7]{III intro}{A correction to the states of the baseline model alone is 
% not sufficient,
% \kwtwo{because missing dynamics need states the baseline does not 
% have\del[M-mail]{
% (Section~\ref{sec:aug_structure})},}
% so additional states are introduced.
\\
The goal is to estimate the \kw{physical and learned parameters} of the
augmented model from $\mathcal D_N$, such that it captures the missing
dynamics and accurately predicts the system, while the identifiable
combinations of the physical parameters are estimated uniquely.
% \mv[Jan23]{IV-C}{The model is trained using short windows of the
% closed-loop data, where each window is simulated with
% \chg[own]{the known controller}{the controller $K_{\mathrm{fb}}$}.
% The initial states are estimated by \chg[Q37]{an encoder}{an encoder network}, 
% including the additional states.}
% \add[M-p7]{\kwtwo{This is the SUBNET method of Beintema et
% al.~\cite{beintema2023subnet}: the encoder estimates each initial state
% from past inputs and outputs and is trained jointly with the model.}}
We use the SUBNET method of Beintema et
al.~\cite{beintema2023subnet} to train the model on short windows of
$\mathcal D_N$, where each window is simulated with the controller
$K_{\mathrm{fb}}$.
The initial states are estimated by an encoder network from past inputs and outputs.

We use the lumped-parameter model of Fig.~\ref{fig:gantry_system} as our
physics-based baseline model of \eqref{eq:system}.
This model does not capture all dynamics of the system.
We identify these missing dynamics from $\mathcal D_N$ and augment the
baseline with learned components and additional
states~\cite{hoekstra2026lfr}.
% \mv[Jan7]{III intro}{A correction to the states of the baseline model alone is 
% not sufficient,
% \kwtwo{because missing dynamics need states the baseline does not 
% have\del[M-mail]{
% (Section~\ref{sec:aug_structure})},}
% so additional states are introduced.
\\
The goal is to estimate the \kw{physical and learned parameters} of the
augmented model from $\mathcal D_N$, such that it captures the missing
dynamics and accurately predicts the system, while the identifiable
combinations of the physical parameters are estimated uniquely.
% \mv[Jan23]{IV-C}{The model is trained using short windows of the
% closed-loop data, where each window is simulated with
% \chg[own]{the known controller}{the controller $K_{\mathrm{fb}}$}.
% The initial states are estimated by \chg[Q37]{an encoder}{an encoder network}, 
% including the additional states.}
% \add[M-p7]{\kwtwo{This is the SUBNET method of Beintema et
% al.~\cite{beintema2023subnet}: the encoder estimates each initial state
% from past inputs and outputs and is trained jointly with the model.}}
We use the SUBNET method of Beintema et
al.~\cite{beintema2023subnet} to train the model on short windows of
$\mathcal D_N$, where each window is simulated with the controller
$K_{\mathrm{fb}}$.
The initial states are estimated by an encoder network from past inputs and outputs.

Garc\'ia-Herreros et al.\ derive the equations of motion of the model
in Fig.~\ref{fig:gantry_system} from the Euler-Lagrange equations
\cite[Eqs.~(3) to~(8)]{garcia2013model}.
Let $L_b$ denote the cross-arm length between the two flexible joints.
The generalised coordinates $q=[X\;\Theta\;Y]^\top$ are defined as 
$X=(X_1+X_2)/2$ and 
$\Theta=(X_1-X_2)/L_b$, the position and yaw angle of
the cross-arm, while $Y$ is unchanged.
% NOTE (2026-10-21, Dirk): Garcia Eq. (1) (PDF p3) defines
%   Theta = asin((X1-X2)/L_b); ours is its small-angle form (sin Theta ~ Theta),

% \kw{These coordinates avoid
% a closed kinematic-chain description and make the coupling 
% associated with the
% \chg[Dirk]{nonuniform load distribution}{\kwtwo{load distribution over $X_1$ and $X_2$, which changes with the payload position $Y$,}} explicit \cite{garcia2013model}.}
These coordinates avoid closed kinematic chains when defining the
kinematics~\cite{garcia2013model}.
They also show the coupling caused by the non-uniform load distribution
between actuators $X_1$ and $X_2$, from the payload and differen

The actuator forces are defined as
$\uact=[F_{X1}\;F_{X2}\;F_Y]^\top$ and the measured positions
$\qact=[X_1\;X_2\;Y]^\top$.
Here $F_{X1}$, $F_{X2}$ and $F_Y$ are the forces and
$X_1$, $X_2$ and $Y$ the measured positions of the
\chg[Dirk]{two X actuators and the Y actuator}{two X and the Y actuators}%
\add[Q17]{\kwtwo{, each from a linear encoder~\cite{garcia2013model}}}.

The system to be identified is the gantry system
described \chg{as,}{by}
\begin{equation}
  \dot x(t)=f\bigl(x(t),\uact(t)\bigr),\qquad y_k=\qact(kT_s)+v_k,
  \label{eq:system}
\end{equation}
% where the \kw{state $x$ is unknown, except that it contains the actuator
% positions $\qact$}, $y_k$ are the measured positions at sample $k$ with
% sampling time $T_s$, and $v_k$ is zero-mean, coloured measurement noise.
% The state-transition function $f$ is unknown.
where the \chg[own]{\kw{state $x$ is unknown, except that it contains the actuator
positions $\qact$}}{state $x$ contains the actuator positions $\qact$}, $y_k$ are the measured positions at sample $k$ with
sampling time $T_s$, and $v_k$ is zero-mean, coloured measurement noise.
The \chg[own]{state-transition function $f$ is}{function $f$ and the
dimension of $x$ are} unknown.
The system runs in closed loop with an assumed known
linear time-invariant feedback controller\del[M-p3]{ (Section~\ref{sec:aug_loop})},
which gives the data set $\mathcal D_N=\{u_{\mathrm{act},k},y_k\}_{k=1}^N$.
% \add[M-p3]{The controller computes the actuator forces from the reference
% $r_k$ and the measured positions, and a feedforward $u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k$ is
% added (Fig.~\ref{fig:system_loop}):}
\add[M-p3]{The controller computes the actuator forces from the
error between the reference $r_k$ and the measured positions $y_k$,
and a feedforward $u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k$ is added (Fig.~\ref{fig:system_loop}):}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 x^{\mathrm{fb}}_{k+1}&=A_{\mathrm{fb}}x^{\mathrm{fb}}_k+B_{\mathrm{fb}}(r_k-y_k),\\
 u_{\mathrm{act},k}&=C_{\mathrm{fb}}x^{\mathrm{fb}}_k+D_{\mathrm{fb}}(r_k-y_k)+u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k,
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:system_loop}
\end{equation}
\mv[M-p3]{IV-B}{where $(A_{\mathrm{fb}},B_{\mathrm{fb}},C_{\mathrm{fb}},D_{\mathrm{fb}})$
are the state-space matrices of the controller\add[own]{ $K_{\mathrm{fb}}$}\add[M-p3]{, with state
$x^{\mathrm{fb}}$,} discretised
with sampling time $T_s$\add[own]{\kwtwo{, and the actuator forces are held
constant between samples, $\uact(t)=u_{\mathrm{act},k}$ for
$kT_s\le t<(k+1)T_s$}}.

%   the second-opinion session sec2-rate-review against Clean/gantry_dynamic
%   and the Simulink model (Dirk 2026-10-21).
Both $r_k$ and $u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k$ are in actuator coordinates.}

\add[M-p3]{The noise $v$ is independent of $r$ and $u^{\mathrm{ff}}$.
The force $u_{\mathrm{act}}$ is correlated with $v$, because the
controller computes it from $y$.}

% NEW (2026-10-21, Dirk): source of the 3x3 matrices; Garcia prints only the
%   2x2 X-Theta matrices, Eqs. (12) to (17). The 3x3 form comes from the ASMPT

Garc\'ia-Herreros et al.\ derive the equations of motion of the model
in Fig.~\ref{fig:gantry_system} from the Euler-Lagrange equations
\cite[Eqs.~(3) to~(8)]{garcia2013model}.
Let $L_b$ denote the cross-arm length between the two flexible joints.
The generalised coordinates $q=[X\;\Theta\;Y]^\top$ are defined as 
$X=(X_1+X_2)/2$ and 
$\Theta=(X_1-X_2)/L_b$, the position and yaw angle of
the cross-arm, while $Y$ is unchanged.
% NOTE (2026-10-21, Dirk): Garcia Eq. (1) (PDF p3) defines
%   Theta = asin((X1-X2)/L_b); ours is its small-angle form (sin Theta ~ Theta),
%   to be made explicit in the small-angle assumption below, not here.
% \kw{These coordinates avoid
% a closed kinematic-chain description and make the coupling 
% associated with the
% \chg[Dirk]{nonuniform load distribution}{\kwtwo{load distribution over $X_1$ and $X_2$, which changes with the payload position $Y$,}} explicit \cite{garcia2013model}.}
These coordinates avoid closed kinematic chains when defining the
kinematics~\cite{garcia2013model}.
They also show the coupling caused by the non-uniform load distribution
between actuators $X_1$ and $X_2$, from the payload and differences in
motor characteristics.

$\qact=[X_1\;X_2\;Y]^\top$.
Here $F_{X1}$, $F_{X2}$ and $F_Y$ are the forces and
$X_1$, $X_2$ and $Y$ the measured positions of the
\chg[Dirk]{two X actuators and the Y actuator}{two X and the Y actuators}%
\add[Q17]{\kwtwo{, each from a linear encoder~\cite{garcia2013model}}}.

The system to be identified is the gantry system
described \chg{as,}{by}
\begin{equation}
  \dot x(t)=f\bigl(x(t),\uact(t)\bigr),\qquad y_k=\qact(kT_s)+v_k,
  \label{eq:system}
\end{equation}
% where the \kw{state $x$ is unknown, except that it contains the actuator
% positions $\qact$}, $y_k$ are the measured positions at sample $k$ with
% sampling time $T_s$, and $v_k$ is zero-mean, coloured measurement noise.
% The state-transition function $f$ is unknown.
where the \chg[own]{\kw{state $x$ is unknown, except that it contains the actuator
positions $\qact$}}{state $x$ contains the actuator positions $\qact$}, $y_k$ are the measured positions at sample $k$ with
sampling time $T_s$, and $v_k$ is zero-mean, coloured measurement noise.
The \chg[own]{state-transition function $f$ is}{function $f$ and the
dimension of $x$ are} unknown.
The system runs in closed loop with an assumed known
linear time-invariant feedback controller\del[M-p3]{ (Section~\ref{sec:aug_loop})},
which gives the data set $\mathcal D_N=\{u_{\mathrm{act},k},y_k\}_{k=1}^N$.
% \add[M-p3]{The controller computes the actuator forces from the reference
% $r_k$ and the measured positions, and a feedforward $u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k$ is
% added (Fig.~\ref{fig:system_loop}):}
\add[M-p3]{The controller computes the actuator forces from the
error between the reference $r_k$ and the measured positions $y_k$,
and a feedforward $u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k$ is added (Fig.~\ref{fig:system_loop}):}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 x^{\mathrm{fb}}_{k+1}&=A_{\mathrm{fb}}x^{\mathrm{fb}}_k+B_{\mathrm{fb}}(r_k-y_k),\\
 u_{\mathrm{act},k}&=C_{\mathrm{fb}}x^{\mathrm{fb}}_k+D_{\mathrm{fb}}(r_k-y_k)+u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k,
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:system_loop}
\end{equation}
\mv[M-p3]{IV-B}{where $(A_{\mathrm{fb}},B_{\mathrm{fb}},C_{\mathrm{fb}},D_{\mathrm{fb}})$
are the state-space matrices of the controller\add[own]{ $K_{\mathrm{fb}}$}\add[M-p3]{, with state
$x^{\mathrm{fb}}$,} discretised
with sampling time $T_s$\add[own]{\kwtwo{, and the actuator forces are held
constant between samples, $\uact(t)=u_{\mathrm{act},k}$ for
$kT_s\le t<(k+1)T_s$}}.

Both $r_k$ and $u^{\mathrm{ff}}_k$ are in actuator coordinates.}

The force $u_{\mathrm{act}}$ is correlated with $v$, because the
controller computes it from $y$.}

We use the lumped-parameter model of Fig.~\ref{fig:gantry_system} as our
physics-based baseline model of \eqref{eq:system}.
This model does not capture all dynamics of the system.
We identify these missing dynamics from $\mathcal D_N$ and augment the
baseline with learned components and additional
states~\cite{hoekstra2026lfr}.
% \mv[Jan7]{III intro}{A correction to the states of the baseline model alone is 
% not sufficient,
% \kwtwo{because missing dynamics need states the baseline does not 
% have\del[M-mail]{
% (Section~\ref{sec:aug_structure})},}
% so additional states are introduced.
\\
The goal is to estimate the \kw{physical and learned parameters} of the
augmented model from $\mathcal D_N$, such that it captures the missing
dynamics and accurately predicts the system, while the identifiable
combinations of the physical parameters are estimated uniquely.
% \mv[Jan23]{IV-C}{The model is trained using short windows of the
% closed-loop data, where each window is simulated with
% \chg[own]{the known controller}{the controller $K_{\mathrm{fb}}$}.
% The initial states are estimated by \chg[Q37]{an encoder}{an encoder network}, 
% including the additional states.}
% \add[M-p7]{\kwtwo{This is the SUBNET method of Beintema et
% al.~\cite{beintema2023subnet}: the encoder estimates each initial state
% from past inputs and outputs and is trained jointly with the model.}}
We use the SUBNET method of Beintema et
al.~\cite{beintema2023subnet} to train the model on short windows of
$\mathcal D_N$, where each window is simulated with the controller
$K_{\mathrm{fb}}$.
The initial states are estimated by an encoder network from past inputs and outputs.

% TODO closed (2026-10-21, Dirk): "state we leave out coulomb friction" is
%   covered by the friction sentence below.
% FEEDBACK (2026-10-21, Dirk): first sentence struck, it repeats Section II
%   (02_system_baseline.tex, "We use the lumped-parameter model of Fig. 1 as

\del[Dirk]{The physics baseline of the gantry system used in this thesis
is the lumped-parameter model of the
dual-drive gantry of Garc\'ia-Herreros et al.~\mbox{\cite{garcia2013model}}.}
% NEW (2026-10-21, Dirk): source of the 3x3 matrices; Garcia prints only the
%   2x2 X-Theta matrices, Eqs. (12) to (17). The 3x3 form comes from the ASMPT
%   implementation (kamtin-fp-model/02 EulerLagrange/EulerLagrange.m).
Garc\'ia-Herreros et al.\ derive the equations of motion of the model
in Fig.~\ref{fig:gantry_system} from the Euler-Lagrange equations
\cite[Eqs.~(3) to~(8)]{garcia2013model}.
Let $L_b$ denote the cross-arm length between the two flexible joints.
The generalised coordinates $q=[X\;\Theta\;Y]^\top$ are defined as 
$X=(X_1+X_2)/2$ and 
$\Theta=(X_1-X_2)/L_b$, the position and yaw angle of
the cross-arm, while $Y$ is unchanged.
% NOTE (2026-10-21, Dirk): Garcia Eq. (1) (PDF p3) defines
%   Theta = asin((X1-X2)/L_b); ours is its small-angle form (sin Theta ~ Theta),
%   to be made explicit in the small-angle assumption below, not here.
% \kw{These coordinates avoid
% a closed kinematic-chain description and make the coupling 
% associated with the
% \chg[Dirk]{nonuniform load distribution}{\kwtwo{load distribution over $X_1$ and $X_2$, which changes with the payload position $Y$,}} explicit \cite{garcia2013model}.}
These coordinates avoid closed kinematic chains when defining the
kinematics~\cite{garcia2013model}.
They also show the coupling caused by the non-uniform load distribution
between actuators $X_1$ and $X_2$, from the payload and differences in
motor characteristics.
% FEEDBACK (2026-10-21, Dirk): todo "How to connect, nonuniform ... moving
%   payload position" resolved: Garcia Sec. 2.2 (PDF p3) attributes the
%   nonuniform load distribution to the payload, and PDF p8 to its variable
%   position; in M(Y) it is the entry (L_b/2)(m_1-m_2)-m_h Y. Todo "why we
%   choose for this realisation" closed: the sentence gives Garcia's reasons
%   (PDF p3).
% FEEDBACK: the green words were Dirk's own, inside the \todo, so the review
%   PDF read "These coordinates avoid [3]." (Jan12, Js26, Q19). Garcia Sec. 2.2
%   gives both reasons.
The coordinate and force transformations are
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
  q &= P^{-\top}\qact,
  \qquad
  u = P\uact,\\
  P &=
  \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & 1 & 0\\
    L_b/2 & -L_b/2 & 0\\
    0 & 0 & 1
  \end{bmatrix},
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:Ptransform}
\end{equation}
where $u$ denotes the generalised force.
